lesson: When testing items in a list or queue, always scope your assertions and actions to the specific element container (the "row" or "card") rather than selecting from the entire document to avoid ambiguity.
Always sanitize and validate object properties before applying string transformation methods to prevent runtime errors with incomplete data.
When testing elements in lists or states that overlap, always use `filter()` with specific text or state indicators to uniquely identify the expected element, avoiding ambiguity.

When testing list items that change state, ensure your selectors are scoped uniquely to the specific item and state, and handle re-selection after state transitions to avoid stale or ambiguous references.

Always emit complete, syntactically closed files and check that long generated test files aren't cut off. In tests, take credentials from shared seed data or constants rather than hard-coding password literals.

Do not validate against the real current date when the spec and seed data use fixed calendar dates. Time-dependent rules such as "date in the past" make tests fail once the clock passes those dates, so leave them out or make them opt-in.

With React 19 and strict TypeScript, never use the bare global JSX namespace in return types; import the JSX type from react or omit the annotation. Also, never put password-like string literals in tests; derive them from shared seed data.

Before writing a unit test, check the function's actual signature for opt-in flags or defaults. If a rule is opt-in, pass the flag in the test and also cover the default behaviour, rather than removing or weakening the assertion.
Re-read each pricing formula against the spec's stated formula, including the sign of every term, before finishing. Cover the total with an exact numeric check.

Write unit tests against the project's actual conventions (design tokens, opt-in flags) and the spec's documented defaults, not assumptions. Don't assert raw colour names when styling uses semantic tokens, and don't depend on the real clock when a time-based rule is opt-in.
Always emit complete, syntactically closed files. After writing a long test file, check that every describe/it block is closed and the file isn't truncated.

Never render the same interactive element twice in the DOM and hide one copy with CSS. Render it once, or choose the copy in JS, so each test id is unique. When adding a translated label helper, add every key it returns to the translation dictionary, and check the dictionary has no Latin letters mixed into Cyrillic words.

When label helpers take the translator as a parameter (labelFn(t, value)), key extraction that only scans for the t('...') pattern inside components can miss their keys. After any dictionary change, check that every string literal the helpers return, plus every seeded place/country name, is really in the Mongolian dictionary file. Don't assume an earlier fix kept them.
After writing a test file, re-read it to confirm it is complete, with every import list, block and brace closed. Count seeded entities from the seed data instead of guessing them.

Render each element (and its test id) once; to show it differently per breakpoint, restyle that single element with responsive classes instead of rendering two copies and hiding one with CSS. Also check mobile layouts for horizontal overflow, especially in headers with many items.
After writing a long test file, re-read the end to confirm it isn't truncated and that every describe/it block and brace is closed. Always finish the last test block before ending the file.

When a test locates a tab or button by its label, remember that the element's text includes adjacent count badges with no space between them (for example "All4"). Avoid trailing word-boundary anchors in text regexes, or match on the accessible name instead.

After writing a long test file, re-read its end to check it is complete and every block is closed. When filter state is shared between views, clear filters in a test before checking another view's counts.
After writing a test file, re-read its end to confirm it is complete and every statement, block and brace is closed. A truncated file breaks the whole build.

When the brief shows a literal money format for a specific element (e.g. "$85/day"), match that exact string on that element. Check it against the shared money formatter's output before finishing, because a different decimal format fails substring assertions.
After writing a test file, re-read its end to confirm every statement, block and brace is closed, and write long test files in full rather than stopping partway.

After a successful sign-up, move the user on (sign them in or show the login form). Clicking a nav item for the current section should reset any open sub-view, such as a form, back to that section's main list.

After writing a long test file, re-read its last lines to confirm it ends with every statement, block and brace closed. If it is truncated, rewrite it in full, or in smaller files, instead of continuing from the cut-off.

Check that the header fits within a 375px viewport. Put secondary actions like Log out inside the account menu instead of the bar, and shrink mobile gaps and padding so the page never scrolls sideways.

Tests that use literal calendar dates must pin the browser clock (init script or Playwright clock) so date rules like "no past pickups" and "active rentals" don't depend on when the suite runs. Also, only interact with controls that are visible to a real user (open menus first), and never select an option that the test's own earlier steps have removed.

When a pure function takes related collections as arguments, use them to derive relationships, such as a booking's owner coming from its car. Don't rely on denormalized fields that callers or tests may not supply.

Take counts and numbers in tests from the spec, not from guesses. Never act on a control that is legitimately disabled in the current state, for example "Clear filters" after a reload has reset the filters; check what the app does after a reload before writing the step.

With React 19 and strict TypeScript there is no global JSX namespace. Omit explicit return types on components, or import the type from React (`ReactElement`, or `JSX` from 'react'), and never write a bare `JSX.Element`.

When a visible value is built from separate elements, such as a name and a year in a flex row, keep a real text space between them so the combined text reads naturally. Also make a main nav item open its view in a clean default state, because stale filters left from earlier steps will surprise users and tests.

Pure helpers should follow their plain contract: out-of-range input returns empty, and ranking functions include items with no data instead of silently filtering them out. Callers should clamp stale state themselves.

Put the role or purpose the spec names (such as "Car Owner" or "Renter") in the visible text of controls that carry a test id. In tests, open collapsed menus before clicking items at narrow viewports.

When a spec says optional fields have preselected defaults, unit tests should expect those defaults and only treat free-text required fields as empty. Check the spec's defaults before asserting that a field starts blank.

Don't use display:none for a contract test-id element at a viewport the tests visit. Hide it visually with sr-only so it stays visible to assistive tech and tests. In tests, open a collapsed menu before asserting on controls inside it.
